records.title: Hypothesis testing of variance and proportions
records.description: Moves from testing means to tests about variances and proportions. The inspected passages link variance tests with chi-square and F distributions and demonstrate proportion calculations in R.
records.provider: NPTEL — National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning

records.title: Hypothesis testing using confidence interval
records.description: Connects confidence intervals with one-sided and two-sided tests, including R output. The inspected examples compare proposed means or proportions with intervals rather than treating the p-value as the only useful result.
records.provider: NPTEL — National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning

records.title: Motivation
records.description: Uses manufacturing examples to turn an informal claim into a statement about a population parameter, then introduces the sequence of a statistical test. The examples concern such quantities as a mean rather than a complete scientific explanation.
records.provider: NPTEL — National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning

records.title: Power of hypothesis test
records.description: Introduces the power of a test through a one-sample mean example. The inspected passages connect power to a specified non-zero effect and to the chance of failing to reject the null under that alternative.
records.provider: NPTEL — National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning

records.title: Probability and Statistics: Review - Part 2
records.description: Extends the probability review to means, variances and joint distributions. The inspected passages discuss combinations of Gaussian variables and the special relationship between zero correlation and independence for jointly Gaussian variables.
records.provider: NPTEL — National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning

records.title: Probability and statistics: Review - Part 1
records.description: Reviews probability, random variables and distribution functions, including how a cumulative distribution describes probabilities. The later inspected passage demonstrates normal-density commands in R.
records.provider: NPTEL — National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning

records.title: R Tutorial 1
records.description: Demonstrates basic R operations with vectors and matrices, including transposition, matrix multiplication and solving linear systems. The inspected sequence also introduces elementary plotting commands.
records.provider: NPTEL — National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning

records.title: Statistic for linear regression
records.description: Introduces statistical inference for a straight-line regression with an intercept and slope. The inspected passages distinguish the fitted model from assumptions about errors and the properties of its estimates.
records.provider: NPTEL — National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning

records.title: Statistics for Hypothesis Testing - Part 1
records.description: Distinguishes a statistic from an estimator and explores how sample means vary across repeated samples. Inspected examples use normal and uniform data in R to make sampling variation visible.
records.provider: NPTEL — National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning

records.title: Statistics for Hypothesis Testing - Part 2
records.description: Continues the discussion of sampling distributions, sample size and properties of estimators. The inspected passages connect sample means with central-limit approximations and discuss chi-square examples.
records.provider: NPTEL — National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning

records.title: Statistics for Variance and Proportion
records.description: Introduces sampling statistics for variances, variance ratios, differences in means and proportions. A comparison of preferences in two campus populations illustrates how the parameter of interest determines the statistical problem.
records.provider: NPTEL — National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning

records.title: Statistics for sample mean
records.description: Separates the spread of observations from the uncertainty of a sample mean. It compares the normal case with finite-sample exponential examples to show why the distribution of the mean and the distribution of individual measurements differ.
records.provider: NPTEL — National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning

records.title: Type I and Type II errors
records.description: Explains false-positive and false-negative decisions in hypothesis testing. An R example repeatedly tests generated samples under a specified null model to connect a significance level with a long-run error rate.
records.provider: NPTEL — National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning

records.title: p value
records.description: Develops p-values and power using rejection regions and a worked propellant example. The inspected passage relates a p-value to a tail probability under a specified null hypothesis.
records.provider: NPTEL — National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning

records.title: Lecture 2 - Foundations: This Is Your Brain
records.description: Introduces dualism and materialism as contrasting accounts of mind and body, followed by basic brain neurophysiology.

records.title: Lecture 4 - Foundations: Skinner

records.title: Lecture 5 - What Is It Like to Be a Baby: The Development of Thought
records.description: Introduces Piaget’s approach and the study of infant cognition, then asks how different kinds of development relate.

records.title: Lecture 6 - How Do We Communicate?: Language in the Brain, Mouth and the Hands
records.description: Introduces language through sounds, word structure, sentence structure and recursion, alongside arguments about acquisition and specialisation.

records.title: Lecture 7 - Conscious of the Present; Conscious of the Past: Language (cont.); Vision and Memory

records.title: Lecture 8 - Conscious of the Present; Conscious of the Past: Vision and Memory (cont.)

records.title: Lecture 10 - Evolution, Emotion, and Reason: Evolution and Rationality
records.description: Introduces an evolutionary perspective on psychology and discusses how evolutionary arguments are used to constrain explanations of behaviour and choice.

records.title: Lecture 11 - Evolution, Emotion, and Reason: Emotions, Part I
records.description: Presents an evolutionary approach to emotion through examples of smiling, fear, family relationships and infants' responses to caregivers.

records.title: Lecture 12 - Evolution, Emotion, and Reason: Emotions, Part II
records.description: Continues an evolutionary interpretation of social emotions, discussing parental love, gratitude, responses to cheating and cultural differences in revenge.

records.title: Lecture 13 - Why Are People Different?: Differences
records.description: Surveys personality and intelligence measurement and the course’s discussion of genetic and environmental explanations for differences between people.

records.title: Lecture 14 - What Motivates Us: Sex

records.title: Lecture 16 - A Person in the World of People: Self and Other, Part I

records.title: Lecture 17 - A Person in the World of People: Self and Other, Part II; Some Mysteries: Sleep, Dreams, and Laughter
records.description: Combines a discussion of social impressions and stereotypes with an introduction to sleep, dreams and theories about laughter.

records.title: Lecture 18 - What Happens When Things Go Wrong: Mental Illness, Part I (Guest Lecture by Professor Susan Nolen-Hoeksema)

records.title: Lecture 19 - What Happens When Things Go Wrong: Mental Illness, Part II
records.description: Discusses definitions of mental illness and several diagnostic groupings before introducing therapy.

records.title: Lecture 20 - The Good Life: Happiness
records.description: Asks how treatment efficacy can be assessed, then turns to happiness, cultural variation and people's predictions about future satisfaction.

records.title: Lecture 06 : Objectives, Steps and Basic Definitions

records.title: Lecture 07 : Variables and Types of Data

records.title: Lecture 08 : Absolute Frequency, Relative Frequency and Frequency Distribution
records.description: Builds absolute and relative frequency tables, moving from category counts to proportions. The checked R material shows how table and length operations implement the denominator used in the summary.

records.title: Lecture 09 : Frequency Distribution and Cumulative Distribution Function
records.description: Groups observations into intervals and constructs frequency and cumulative-frequency summaries. The inspected race-time example uses R operations such as cut and table to show how grouping decisions become calculations.

records.title: Lecture 10 : Bar Diagrams
records.description: Creates bar diagrams from frequency tables and relative frequencies. The inspected examples show how category counts, denominators, labels and graphical parameters affect the resulting display in R.

records.title: Lecture 15 : Median

records.title: Lecture 16 : Quantiles

records.title: Lecture 1 - Introduction: Five First Lessons
records.description: Introduces strategic interaction by separating players, available actions and payoffs, then comparing a prisoners’ dilemma with a coordination problem.

records.title: Lecture 2 - Putting Yourselves into Other People's Shoes
records.description: Develops strategic reasoning through dominated strategies, assumptions about other players and the distinction between knowledge and common knowledge.

records.title: Lecture 3 - Iterative Deletion and the Median-Voter Theorem
records.description: Applies repeated elimination of dominated strategies to a model of electoral competition and introduces choosing a best response to a belief about another player.

records.title: Lecture 4 - Best Responses in Soccer and Business Partnerships
records.description: Works through best responses using penalty kicks and a profit-sharing partnership, leading towards the idea of Nash equilibrium.

records.title: Lecture 5 - Nash Equilibrium: Bad Fashion and Bank Runs
records.description: Defines Nash equilibrium and uses an investment game to examine coordination, multiple equilibria and undesirable collective outcomes.

records.title: Lecture 6 - Nash Equilibrium: Dating and Cournot
records.description: Applies Nash equilibrium to a coordination game and to Cournot competition, discussing collusion and the consequences of different market arrangements.

records.title: Lecture 7 - Nash Equilibrium: Shopping, Standing and Voting on a Line
records.description: Compares price competition with spatial models of customers and voters, including a classroom candidate-entry game.

records.title: Lecture 8 - Nash Equilibrium: Location, Segregation and Randomization
records.description: Moves from electoral location to Schelling’s segregation game and then introduces randomised choices through mixed strategies.

records.title: Lecture 9 - Mixed Strategies in Theory and Tennis
records.description: Uses tennis to derive mixed-strategy equilibria and explains why the pure strategies used in an optimal mixture must have equal expected payoffs.

records.title: Lecture 10 - Mixed Strategies in Baseball, Dating and Paying Your Taxes
records.description: Distinguishes three interpretations of mixed strategies: actual randomisation, uncertainty about a player and proportions of a population using different actions.

records.title: Lecture 11 - Evolutionary Stability: Cooperation, Mutation, and Equilibrium
records.description: Introduces evolutionary stability and relates it to domination and Nash equilibrium. Yale flags a notation error in the informal argument and supplies a correction in the accompanying notes.

records.title: Lecture 12 - Evolutionary Stability: Social Convention, Aggression, and Cycles
records.description: Applies evolutionary stability to conventions and Hawk–Dove games, then considers a setting without an evolutionarily stable population.

records.title: Lecture 13 - Sequential Games: Moral Hazard, Incentives, and Hungry Lions
records.description: Introduces sequential decisions and backward induction through lending, incentives and commitment examples.

records.title: Lecture 14 - Backward Induction: Commitment, Spies, and First-Mover Advantages
records.description: Applies backward induction to sequential quantity competition and examines how commitment and information affect apparent first-mover advantages.

records.title: Lecture 15 - Backward Induction: Chess, Strategies, and Credible Threats
records.description: Discusses solutions to finite perfect-information games, defines strategies in sequential games and examines equilibrium threats that may not be credible.

records.title: Lecture 16 - Backward Induction: Reputation and Duels
records.description: Studies reputation in the chain-store paradox and a pre-emption game, using uncertainty about other players to revisit credible promises and threats.

records.title: Lecture 17 - Backward Induction: Ultimatums and Bargaining
records.description: Builds a bargaining model from ultimatum offers to alternating offers, making patience, discounting and knowledge of the bargaining surplus explicit.

records.title: Lecture 18 - Imperfect Information: Information Sets and Sub-Game Perfection
records.description: Uses information sets to represent what players cannot distinguish, then introduces subgame perfection for games with sequential and simultaneous components.

records.title: Lecture 19 - Subgame Perfect Equilibrium: Matchmaking and Strategic Investments
records.description: Applies subgame-perfect equilibrium to examples involving mistakes, matchmaking and investment, including how an investment changes competitors’ choices.

records.title: Lecture 20 - Subgame Perfect Equilibrium: Wars of Attrition
records.description: Analyses wars of attrition in short and potentially continuing games, asking why costly conflict can persist under particular rational-choice assumptions.

records.title: Lecture 21 - Repeated Games: Cooperation vs. the End Game
records.description: Examines repeated games, end-of-game incentives and the use of future outcomes to sustain present cooperation.

records.title: Lecture 22 - Repeated Games: Cheating, Punishment, and Outsourcing
records.description: Continues repeated-game analysis with credible rewards and punishments, contrasting severe and milder punishment strategies as relationships endure.

records.title: Lecture 23 - Asymmetric Information: Silence, Signaling and Suffering Education
records.description: Studies communication under asymmetric information, contrasting verifiable disclosure with costly signals and discussing education as a signalling example.

records.title: Lecture 24 - Asymmetric Information: Auctions and the Winner's Curse
records.description: Compares auction formats and distinguishes common-value from private-value settings, using a classroom auction to introduce the winner’s curse.

records.title: Why Do We Love? - Robin May
records.description: Explores biological explanations of romantic and parental love. Broad empirical claims in the transcript need separate scientific assessment before being repeated as conclusions.

records.title: Intro
records.description: Introduces the biological complexity behind neuron and synapse models, including electrical signalling and the route into simplified computational descriptions.

records.title: Intro
records.description: Neuromatch’s Model Types introduction distinguishes descriptive, mechanistic and principle-seeking modelling goals using neuronal inter-spike intervals as a shared example.

records.title: Video 1: Dynamic networks
records.description: Introduces rate-based neural networks and an input-to-firing-rate relation for a single population of neurons.

records.title: Video 1: Fixed points and their stability
records.description: Extends the two-population model to fixed points, local stability, oscillatory behaviour and inhibition-stabilised regimes.

records.title: Video 1: Input & output correlations
records.description: Connects correlated inputs with correlations in neuronal outputs, supported by exercises using pairs of simplified spiking neurons.

records.title: Video 1: Linear Regression & Mean Squared Error
records.description: Introduces linear regression and mean squared error within a Neuromatch tutorial that asks learners to calculate error and fit a model parameter.

records.title: Video 1: Phase analysis of the Wilson-Cowan E-I model
records.description: Introduces the Wilson–Cowan model of interacting excitatory and inhibitory populations and its two-dimensional phase plane.

records.title: Video 1: Reduced Neuron Models
records.description: Introduces the reduction of a biological neuron to a leaky integrate-and-fire model, paired with a written explanation of its assumptions and a coding exercise.

records.title: Video 1: STDP
records.description: Introduces a synaptic learning model in which weight changes depend on the relative timing of pre- and postsynaptic spikes.

records.title: Video 1: Static and dynamic synapses
records.description: Introduces static and dynamic synapses, with a notebook that contrasts fixed connection strengths with short-term facilitation and depression.

records.title: Video 1: “What” Models
records.description: Introduces the descriptive-model section of a Neuromatch tutorial that explores spike recordings, visualisation and inter-spike-interval distributions.

records.title: Video 2: Fixed point
records.description: Introduces recurrent networks, fixed points and a one-dimensional phase description of changing activity.

records.title: Video 2: Nullclines and Vector Fields
records.description: Uses nullclines and vector fields to describe the directions in which excitatory and inhibitory population activity changes.

records.title: Video 2: Response of ensemble of neurons to time-varying input
records.description: A bonus lecture on how an ensemble of neurons responds to input that varies over time, following a tutorial about shared inputs and correlations.

records.title: Video 2: Response of the LIF neuron to different inputs
records.description: Introduces responses of a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron to different inputs, alongside demonstrations using constant and noisy currents.

records.title: Video 3: Stability of fixed points
records.description: Explains local stability by considering whether a small perturbation around a fixed point grows or decays.

records.title: How do you turn a question into a testable experiment?
records.description: Connect a question, a measure, a comparison and an analysis before collecting observations.
terms: How do you turn a research question into a testable experiment?

records.title: How can you tell whether a measure is reliable and valid?
records.description: Separate what a score records, how consistently it behaves and which interpretation the evidence supports.
terms: How can you tell whether a measure is reliable and valid?

records.title: When can a study support a causal explanation?
records.description: Separate an observed relationship from a specified intervention contrast and inspect the assumptions connecting them.
terms: When can a study support a causal explanation?

records.title: How does social attachment work across species?
records.description: Distinguish kinds of relationship and connect behavioural, physiological, developmental and ecological questions.
terms: How does social attachment work across species?

records.title: How can a model help explain neural activity?
records.description: Connect modelling goals, simplified neuronal mechanisms, spike data and fitting exercises, with an optional route into network models.
terms: How do we choose, build and test a model for a neuroscience question?

records.title: How does attention shape what we notice?
records.description: Move from selection and perceptual tasks to competing accounts of attention, measurement and the separate question of awareness.
terms: How can an experiment distinguish attention, perception and awareness?

records.title: How can evolutionary explanations of human behaviour be tested?
records.description: Separate mechanism, development, ancestry and possible function, then ask which comparative observations could distinguish rival accounts.
terms: How can evolutionary explanations of human behaviour be tested?

records.title: How can we study what a human brain is doing?
records.description: Compare measurement approaches, experimental contrasts and interpretational limits before following a specialist brain-imaging or connectivity route.
terms: What can different neuroscience methods tell us, and what would make an experiment informative?

records.title: What do glial cells contribute beyond supporting neurons?
records.description: Use microglia as a research example while preserving the distinction between different glial cell types.
terms: What do glial cells contribute beyond supporting neurons?

records.title: What makes a therapy trial informative?
records.description: Work through comparison, assignment, outcomes, masking and generalisation using an original study-design exercise.
terms: What makes a therapy trial informative?

records.title: How can we investigate consciousness in other animals?
records.description: Compare evidence about experience with evidence about particular behavioural abilities, while making alternative explanations explicit.
terms: How can we investigate consciousness in other animals?

records.title: How do synapses change a circuit’s response?
records.description: Separate transmission, short-term changes and longer-term learning rules before moving to networks.
terms: How do synapses change a circuit’s response?

records.title: What can a confidence interval or hypothesis test tell you?
records.description: Connect sampling variation, test behaviour and interval estimates without turning them into probabilities that a scientific claim is true.
terms: What can a confidence interval or hypothesis test actually tell you?

records.title: How does a neuron generate an electrical signal?
records.description: Follow a membrane signal from moving ions to a deliberately simplified model of a spike.
terms: How does a neuron generate an electrical signal?

records.title: How do specialised brain areas work as systems?
records.description: Connect anatomy, activity relationships and circuit models without confusing one for another.
terms: How do specialised brain areas work as systems?

records.title: How do transparent choices make a result more reproducible?
records.description: Connect explicit analysis decisions and readable computation with the separate tasks of reproducing a result and testing a claim again.
terms: How do transparent analysis choices make a result more reproducible?

records.title: What can—and cannot—we learn by comparing brains across species?
records.description: Move from brain size and proportional scaling to cellular development and task-specific behaviour, without turning the comparison into a ranking of intelligence.
terms: What can—and cannot—we learn by comparing brains across species?

records.title: How does the nervous system control movement?
records.description: Organise movement questions across motor units, spinal circuits and higher systems.
terms: How does the nervous system control movement?

records.title: Read a quantitative paper critically
records.description: A ten-step reading sequence that moves from the recorded variables and descriptive patterns to the tested parameter, uncertainty, model assumptions and prediction claims. Use the linked causal and transparency readings for questions the statistical calculation cannot answer.

records.title: Comparing minds across species without a single ladder
records.description: Move from scaling and task design to development, field behaviour and human origins. Each step changes one part of the comparison so that the final synthesis is a research plan, not a ranking of species.

records.title: From neurons and spike data to network models
records.description: Begin with physical and circuit models, connect them to synapses and spike data, then extend to receptive fields and recurrent memory models. Each step asks what the representation includes and what observation would challenge it. This is a selected route, with the full course available for omitted derivations.

records.title: From membranes to interacting circuits
records.description: This route follows the mechanism of communication: charge movement, membrane response, transmission and interacting populations. It differs from a general introduction to computational neuroscience by organising every step around what changes between an input and an output. Begin with conceptual sketches, then use the mathematical and notebook material only as preparation allows. The recurring task is to identify what is measured, what is modelled and what the model omits.

records.title: Following a movement system from muscle to brain
records.description: Work upwards through the dedicated human-movement course: motor units, spinal circuits and higher systems. The order preserves the relevant official course sequence while omitting unrelated lessons for a manageable first route. Each task adds to one labelled explanation of a hypothetical reach. Anatomical assignments remain tentative until supported; the aim is to connect levels, not memorise a different structure at every stop.

records.title: From a brain question to an experiment
records.description: Follow the Human Brain course from its central questions through methods, experimental design and competing interpretations. The route preserves the relevant lecture order and adds a continuing task: refine one question into two discriminating experiments.

records.title: Design and evaluate a behavioural study
records.description: An eight-step route from a population and outcome to a comparison, power assumptions and an interpretable interval. The associated guide and design readings supply the experimental-design concepts that the statistics demonstrations do not cover.

records.title: What can a redshift tell us about motion?
records.description: Follow the change in spacing between successive wave crests as a source recedes. The period measured by the observer is the time between arrivals. Which clock supplies that interval?
terms: Lecture 3: The Doppler Effect and Special Relativity
Lecture 4: The Kinematics of the Homogeneous Expanding Universe

records.title: What sets the speed of air–sea gas exchange?
records.description: A gas can be far from equilibrium with seawater and still enter it slowly. Listen for the distinction between the concentration the water could support and the rate at which molecules cross the interface.
terms: Session 11: Gas Exchange Across the Air-sea Interface

records.title: When does mixing fail to explain estuary chemistry?
records.description: Start with two water masses. If mixing is the only process, each dissolved constituent has a concentration fixed by the fraction of each water mass present. A reaction can move an observation away from that prediction.
terms: Session 10: Non-conservative Processes in Estuaries/ Groundwater/Hydrothermal
Session 11: Gas Exchange Across the Air-sea Interface

records.title: Can two processes transfer different amounts of heat between the same states?
records.description: Listen for how a boundary lets energy cross as heat or work. A state measurement can constrain their combined effect while leaving the history of the process open.
terms: Lecture 3: Process Variables and the First Law
Lecture 5: Second Law and Entropy Maximization

records.title: Why does an isolated system approach equilibrium?
records.description: The entropy-maximisation argument requires a boundary condition. Track what can move between subsystems, what remains fixed for the whole, and where the extremum is taken.
terms: Lecture 5: Second Law and Entropy Maximization

records.title: When can an entire circuit be replaced by two components?
records.description: Begin with the junction and loop equations. They let you predict what an external load will measure without observing every internal current.

records.title: Why can honeycombs made of the same material have different stiffnesses?
records.description: Look at the direction and thickness of the cell walls. An applied force can stretch one wall and bend another, even when both walls are made of the same solid.
terms: Cellular Solids: Structure, Properties and Applications

records.title: How does a solar cell turn light into current?
records.description: In the photoconductivity tutorial, separate the creation of mobile charge carriers from their movement. An increase in conductivity does not by itself specify which terminal will collect the electrons.

records.title: Why does merge sort scale differently from insertion sort?
records.description: Watch the recursion tree take shape. The amount of work at a single level and the number of levels answer different counting questions.

records.title: What makes a feedback signal decay or grow?
records.description: Follow a single value around a delay loop. The delay determines when it returns and the gain determines how much comes back. A block diagram can make both easier to trace than an expanded sequence.
terms: Lecture 3: Feedback, Poles, and Fundamental Modes

records.title: When does flowing water carry sediment in suspension?
records.description: Track the distinction between material travelling near the bed and material carried within the water column. A sampler near the surface and one at the bed can give different impressions of the same flow.
terms: Fluid Motions, Sediment Transport, and Current-Generated Sedimentary Structures

records.title: How can layers of rock record the direction of an ancient current?
records.description: Begin with a moving bedform. A dune has a shape at an instant and a history of migration. The layers it leaves behind need not preserve the whole shape.
terms: Lecture 4: Sedimentary Structures Produced by Sediment Transport
Fluid Motions, Sediment Transport, and Current-Generated Sedimentary Structures

records.title: Where did the elements in a star come from?
records.description: Start by separating a census of elements from an explanation of their origin. The abundance of an element in a star is an observation that a history of production, mixing and incorporation must explain.
terms: Episode 2. What the Universe Is Made Of
Cosmic Origin of the Chemical Elements

records.title: What evidence could identify an early episode of chemical enrichment?
records.description: Consider how a first generation of stars can leave traces in material that formed later. The chemical pattern of a surviving star integrates events before its birth.
terms: Episode 4: The First Chemical Enrichment Events
Cosmic Origin of the Chemical Elements

records.title: Why do thin films show different colours at different angles?
records.description: Watch for colour changes as viewing geometry changes. Light reflected at the two faces of a film travels along different optical paths. The relative phase depends on the paths and the wavelength.
terms: Lecture 2: Reflection and refraction; prisms, waveguides, and dispersion

records.title: Which data can tell a transit planner why a route looks empty?
records.description: Count passengers at one stop, on one vehicle and over an entire day. Each count has a different denominator. A quiet observation can reflect timing or sampling as easily as demand.
terms: Lecture 2: Data Collection Techniques and Program Design

records.title: Where does a lens form an image?
records.description: Trace a small group of rays from one object point. The paraxial approximation makes an off-axis ray easier to predict near the optical axis. Ask which rays you would inspect first to find the approximation breaking down.
terms: Lecture 3: Focusing, imaging, and the paraxial approximation
Lecture 4: Sign conventions; thin lenses; real and virtual images

records.title: Why can two observers disagree about simultaneity?
records.description: Separate an event from the time a signal from that event reaches an observer. The history of special relativity asks what measurements would justify assigning a common time to spatially separated events.
terms: Lecture 3: The Doppler Effect and Special Relativity

records.title: When does a force change angular momentum?
records.description: Begin with the free-body diagram and identify which object each force acts upon. A force can change linear momentum while its torque about a chosen point is zero.
terms: A review of Newton's three laws of motion
Angular momentum of a particle, torque as the time rate of change of angular momentum, and the appearance of the coriolis force

records.title: What kinds of explanation can answer one question about animal behaviour?
records.description: Tinbergen’s questions let a single observation support several lines of inquiry. A stimulus that initiates a display and the possible reproductive consequences of that display call for different evidence.
terms: Lec4: Ethology and Konrad Lorenz' Jackdaws

records.title: What must a probability model count as an outcome?
records.description: Start with the sample space before assigning probabilities. Describing a pair of coin tosses by the number of heads discards the order of the tosses and changes which events can be expressed.

records.title: How can a conservation law survive a change of coordinates?
records.description: A vector and its components play different roles when a coordinate basis changes. Follow the basis through the introduction of four-vectors, then ask which physical statement both descriptions must preserve.
terms: Lecture 4: Volumes and Volume Elements; Conservation Laws

records.title: Why does compactness matter beyond ordinary Euclidean space?
records.description: Start with the Euclidean result and identify exactly where the ambient space enters. A familiar test involving closed and bounded sets can hide assumptions about the metric and dimension.

records.title: What does a matrix factorisation reveal about dependent columns?
records.description: Watch the independent columns get selected during elimination. The coefficients describing the remaining columns tell you how to reconstruct all of the original data from a smaller set of columns.

records.title: How can two different tones give the same digital samples?
records.description: Oppenheim’s demonstration lets you compare a continuous sinusoid with its values on a sampling grid. A sample records the signal at one instant and says nothing directly about the path between instants.
terms: Demonstration 1: Sampling, Aliasing, and Frequency Response, Part 1
Demonstration 2: Sampling, Aliasing, and Frequency Response, Part 2

records.title: What changes when an energy model moves from the planet to one house?
records.description: In the systems demonstration, identify an input the modeller changes and an outcome the model computes. The connection between them depends on the boundary chosen for the energy system.
terms: Session 1-1: A Systems View of the Energy Transition and Role of Methane Emissions
Session 1-2: Carbon Reduction Pathways for Building Stocks
Geothermal Energy Networks: Transforming Our Thermal Energy System

records.title: How can a ray matrix predict the path through a camera lens?
records.description: Represent a ray by its height and angle at a reference plane. Propagation and refraction each change that pair. Following the ray element by element makes the ordering of the optical system explicit.
terms: Lecture 2: Modern optics and lenses; ray-matrix operations; context enhanced imaging - Part 1
Lecture 2: Modern optics and lenses; ray-matrix operations; context enhanced imaging - Part 2

records.title: Can a moving camera estimate time to contact from an expanding image?
records.description: Follow the projection of an approaching object onto the image plane. A single apparent size confounds size and distance. Its rate of change supplies another piece of evidence under assumptions about motion.
terms: Lecture 2: Image Formation, Perspective Projection, Time Derivative, Motion Field
Lecture 3: Time to Contact, Focus of Expansion, Direct Motion Vision Methods, Noise Gain

records.title: What does a computer need to represent a melody?
records.description: A recording, a list of pitches and a score preserve different properties of a performance. Follow the live coding example and ask what information must already have been extracted before the program can compare notes.
terms: Class 1 Video: How Do Computers "Hear" Music?
Class 2 Video: Representation of Notes, Pitches, and Durations

records.title: What does a two-slit pattern tell us about an electron?
records.description: Begin with the wave description of the electron. Distinguish a prediction about the distribution of many detections from a prediction of the exact position of a single detection.
terms: Lecture 2: Wave Nature of the Electron and the Internal Structure of an Atom

records.title: How can resonance help measure a frequency?
records.description: Begin with the classical resonance of a driven oscillator. The natural frequency, the driving frequency and the width of the response peak describe different features of the experiment.

records.title: From starlight to stellar ancestry
records.description: For astronomy students using light to infer the history of a stellar population. Build an argument from wavelength shift, elemental abundance and enrichment.

records.title: From an estuary to the atmosphere
records.description: For Earth science students tracing material across system boundaries. Distinguish mixing, gas transfer and the longer cycle.

records.title: Read the record of a river
records.description: For geology learners interpreting a sedimentary outcrop. Reconstruct transport, bed shape and preservation before assigning a flow direction.

records.title: Follow energy through a device
records.description: For engineering students learning to choose a system boundary. Account for heat, carrier generation and electrical output.

records.title: From atomic behaviour to bulk properties
records.description: For materials students deciding which physical scale explains a measurement. Move from an electron, to a semiconductor, to the walls of a structured solid.

records.title: Trace light through an instrument
records.description: For optics students who can sketch rays. Separate the direction of a ray, its phase and its contribution to an image.

records.title: From moving images to measurements
records.description: For computing students building intuition for sensor data. Work from image formation to image motion and then test the sampling assumptions.

records.title: Study a signal in time and frequency
records.description: For students with elementary algebra. Trace a feedback recurrence, estimate a peak frequency and explain a sampling ambiguity.

records.title: From a coordinate choice to a conservation law
records.description: For physics students moving from Newtonian mechanics to relativity. Distinguish a choice of origin from a measurable change in momentum.

records.title: Choose a mathematical representation
records.description: For students preparing for proof-based courses. Decide what information is preserved by a sample space, a factorisation and a metric.

records.title: Design a comparison from observations
records.description: For learners planning a small field study. Define the outcome, devise a sampling plan and distinguish competing types of explanation.

records.title: Represent sound for computation
records.description: For musicians and programmers exploring digital audio. Move between a continuous tone, samples and symbolic notes before choosing how to order records.

records.title: What survives of a technology?
records.description: A stone flake, a charred seed and a surviving length of cord answer different questions about human skill. Begin with the Smithsonian’s comparison of stone, bone and plant remains.
terms: Compare marks on bone with experimental examples. Matching marks can support an inference about use even when the implement itself is missing.
Put Kuk Swamp beside the Andes. Ask what a drainage feature, a starch grain and the remains of a meal can each establish about tending a plant.
The occupation of Sahul requires a sea crossing. Modern Pacific wayfinding helps explain the knowledge a crossing can require. It cannot identify the route taken by the earliest travellers.

Compare the surviving cord from Abri du Maras with a living tradition of bridge renewal in the Andes. Use the bridge to ask about fibres, inspection and collective labour. The modern practice cannot establish what the prehistoric cord was for.

What can a fired object reveal about the maker’s control over heat? Compare an early ceramic object with the much later evidence for Greek pots. Separate what can be inferred from the fired body from what depends on evidence for the workshop.

records.title: How can an institution make a quantity travel?
records.description: Early urban societies had to move goods, divide work and keep records that another person could read. An account is evidence both for quantities and for the people who had reason to count.
terms: Examine the Sumerian tablet that records malt and groats. Which distinctions would matter to the storehouse but disappear in a single total for grain?
The Uluburun cargo brings copper and tin together at sea. A cargo establishes movement; the place where someone cast the finished object needs independent evidence.
An Egyptian water clock could be marked for use at different times of year. Ask what its graduations say about the definition of an hour.
Follow the book from the household to the street drain. Compare that urban scale with a qanat linking groundwater to a settlement. Which remains would reveal maintenance as well as construction?
Compare a drawing of an object with an account recording a quantity. Ask whether the units, recipient and date could be recovered by someone outside the recording institution.

records.title: When does a repeated observation become a calculation?
records.description: Astronomers, physicians, builders and mathematical teachers had different reasons to preserve procedures. Ask what a reader would need to repeat a result away from its author.
terms: Compare Babylonian series of observations with a modern spectrum. Both preserve differences for later comparison, but they measure different properties of the sky.
Archimedes related displacement to a body’s behaviour in water. Sketch the forces on a floating object and identify which quantities an observer could weigh.
Follow the book from papermaking to the movement of technical instructions. Compare the knowledge preserved in a written direction with the tacit judgement needed to make the material itself.
Read the St Andrews account of the Chinese Nine Chapters. Take one problem about distributing goods or measuring land. Before calculating, list the quantities known and the one sought.
Trace a load through a Roman vault. How did working with concrete change the shapes a builder could enclose? What can the finished interior tell us about the construction sequence?
How could a coherent theory of the body influence what a practitioner recorded? Read the book’s medical examples alongside Yale’s lecture on Hippocrates, Galen and humoralism.

records.title: What changes when knowledge crosses languages?
records.description: A translation, an instrument and a set of recorded quantities carry different parts of a practice. Follow examples from the Islamic world, West Africa and the Andes.
terms: Use the Met’s teaching on Islamic astronomy to connect an instrument with local time and direction. Which settings must change when the observer moves?

Study the Great Mosque of Djenné as a building maintained by a community. Compare what its surface reveals with what must be learned from the history of replacement and repair. The standing mosque is later than its medieval predecessors.
Examine an Inka khipu. Separate the position and form of a knot from the identity of the goods or people being counted. The book’s Andean sequence extends across the period boundary.
Follow the distinctions between an empty position, a written placeholder and a number with arithmetic rules. Ask which of the three a particular inscription can demonstrate.
Compare a surviving Arabic alchemical text with a surviving vessel. Decide what each tells us about the movement of vocabulary and about work actually performed.

records.title: How did print and instruments change who could check a claim?
records.description: A printed diagram could reach distant readers. A navigational observation still depended on who took it, where they stood and how the instrument was set.
terms: Compare the repeatability of a printed anatomical figure with the variation between bodies. Which features could later readers check without consulting the same specimen?
Compare a recorded altitude with Pacific wayfinding. Identify which observations depend on the season and which require close familiarity with local conditions.
Trace two rays from a distant point through a lens. Use the construction to ask how an observer might distinguish an object in the sky from an imperfection in the instrument.
Examine a Benin court plaque and the evidence for traded brass. Distinguish the movement of the metal from the local authority, skills and purposes that shaped the object.
Who could use a printed page?
Yale’s lecture distinguishes different kinds of literacy in early modern England. Compare the skills required to recognise a printed notice, read an unfamiliar argument and write a reply.

records.title: What makes a measurement or machine work somewhere else?
records.description: Compare three ways to make a claim portable: an optical arrangement another person can repeat, a clock that travels and an engine design that saves heat.
terms: Draw the path of one part of a spectrum into a second prism. Ask what observation would distinguish colour already separated from colour introduced by the glass.
A clock taken to sea had to preserve a reference time while a navigator measured local time. Which errors would accumulate during a long voyage?
Follow the steam from cylinder to condenser. Separating hot and cold parts changed how much fuel the engine consumed for a given task.
Use Yale’s economic history teaching to ask who could finance a change in equipment or secure a market for its output. A working machine and a widely adopted machine leave different records.

records.title: How could an instrument or a table expose a hidden regularity?
records.description: Industry gave researchers new materials, more precise instruments and pressing questions about heat and power. Some of the strongest claims came from patterns with a conspicuous gap.
terms: Use spectroscopy to distinguish a repeatable dark line from a change in overall brightness. Explain why a comparison spectrum is useful.
Compare the history of the periodic table with a modern lecture on periodic trends. Which predictions would have been risky before the element was found?
Consider a mechanical input that produces a temperature rise. Specify the system boundary before comparing the work supplied with the heating observed.
Compare a case narrative with a hospital series. Changing who enters hospital can change an apparent treatment outcome even if the treatment is unchanged.

records.title: What evidence could connect an invisible process to a visible effect?
records.description: A signal on a wire, a fringe in an interferometer and a change in the course of illness all require interpretation. Instruments and institutions influence what can be detected.
terms: Follow the loads on a network with Kirchhoff’s circuit laws. Ask how one subscriber’s demand could alter the voltage at another connection.
Use “An interferometer constrains the ether wind” to compare an expected fringe shift with the measured bound. A small result can put a number on the size of an effect compatible with the apparatus.
Use Frank Snowden’s course to compare explanations of epidemic disease with the decisions taken by health authorities. Consider what mortality records leave out.
Compare a successful sanitary measure with the theory originally offered for it. What observation would bear on the mechanism rather than only on the outcome?

records.title: How can a trace stand in for an event too small or fast to see?
records.description: Tracks, diffraction patterns and grouped outcomes took investigators from individual marks to competing explanations. Their interpretation required models of the measuring system.
terms: In the book’s particle-direction problem, a track crosses a plate. Compare its curvature on the two sides. Which inference depends on knowing that the particle lost energy?
Start with the two-slit lecture. Separate the position of a single detection from the pattern accumulated over many trials.
Use the lesson on randomised experiments to distinguish a difference between groups from an effect of treatment. Consider what a field boundary or admission rule could change.
Connect the book’s treatment of ecosystems to Yale’s teaching on the evolution of behaviour. Ask which observation concerns one animal and which would require a population followed over time.

records.title: How did researchers learn to read a planet or a molecule through instruments?
records.description: Measurements taken in one place could bear on a much larger system. The challenge was to distinguish a local disturbance from a pattern that persisted across instruments or sites.
terms: Trace matching bands on opposing sides of a ridge, then compare the model with “Would you fund the next seafloor test?” in Historical judgement.
Compare a seasonal oscillation with a rising baseline in the Mauna Loa figure in “Separating a rising carbon-dioxide record from local air”. Ask which measurements would reveal local contamination.
A switch made from a solid
Read the Computer History Museum’s semiconductor chronology. Distinguish a working device from a process that could produce thousands with comparable properties.
Separate identifying DNA as hereditary material from explaining how its structure could support copying. Put each claim beside the kind of evidence needed to support it.

records.title: When can a network or a global record be trusted?
records.description: A successful transfer across two computers establishes interoperability for that exchange. A decades-long environmental record raises a different question about continuity across instruments.
terms: Follow the Internet History collection from linked networks to shared conventions. Decide what two independently implemented systems would need to demonstrate before a conversion.
Compare NASA’s sequence of Antarctic maps at the same season across years. Identify the difference between the annual cycle and a long-term change.
Read “Repairing a telescope by correcting its light” and follow the focusing lecture. Explain why changing the light path could correct a fault in a mirror left in orbit.
Compare the evidence for a molecular change with evidence for its frequency in a population. What can a study of one family establish, and what requires differently sampled people?

records.title: How far can a striking result be generalised?
records.description: A first image, a laboratory efficiency result and a storage demonstration establish different things. Ask how the system boundary and the comparison change between demonstration and routine use.
terms: Inspect Webb’s first deep field. Distinguish foreground stars, cluster members and images of more distant sources distorted by gravitational lensing.

Compare the small cell in “Tandem cells divide sunlight between two absorbers” with the collection of carriers in a single junction. Explain why a record on a small area leaves questions about modules and service life.
Compare the energy a store can hold with the power it can supply. Which quantity limits a short interruption and which limits a prolonged shortage?
Read the account of closing gaps in a human genome. Explain why completeness of an individual sequence and representation of variation between people answer different questions.
Inspect the two gravitational-wave signals. Ask how their relative timing, shape and local noise records affect the claim that both detectors registered the same distant event.

records.title: Crops across the Indian Ocean
records.description: When does a grain establish contact between communities?
terms: Start with the difference between a seed recovered in a settlement and one directly dated. Put the Sahelian origin and the Sindh find on a map. The route between them remains a further inference.
Three charred grains in Sindh: tracing a Sahelian cereal to the Indus

records.title: From counting to a planetary orbit
records.description: How did a numerical record become an orbital test?
terms: From counting to a planetary orbit

Compare keeping a consistent astronomical series with fitting a geometrical model. Kepler’s area law predicts unequal speeds at different parts of an orbit. Identify an observation that would separate it from uniform motion.
From Babylonian reckoning to the shape of Mars’s orbit

records.title: Anatomy on the page
records.description: What could a reader verify in a printed body?
terms: Trace the transfer from dissection to drawing, block and page. Use the spinal anatomy lecture to distinguish a recurring structure from a feature peculiar to a specimen or a printed view.
From Alexandrian dissection to the printed body

records.title: From a reading glass to a molecular image
records.description: Which features belong to the specimen and which to the instrument?
terms: From a reading glass to a molecular image
Compare magnifying an object with increasing the separation of details that can be resolved. At each stage ask how sample preparation and the reconstruction of an image might change what appears.
From reading glasses to a frozen virus

records.title: Counting deaths and documenting eradication
records.description: What does an empty column in a health return establish?
terms: Follow a case from local detection to a population count. Give two reasons a district might report zero cases and one independent way to distinguish them.
From burial returns to the end of smallpox

records.title: From an eclipse delay to a conservation law
records.description: How can timing become a test of physical theory?
terms: From an eclipse delay to a conservation law
A moon can keep a regular orbit while its eclipses arrive late to a distant observer. Separate emission time from arrival time before comparing the predictions of different descriptions of motion.
From the late eclipses of Jupiter’s moon to the conservation of energy

records.title: Melting ice and engine efficiency
records.description: Which constraint limits the useful work an engine can deliver?
terms: Compare heating that changes temperature with heating that changes phase. Then trace energy through an engine cycle and account for the heat that leaves it.
From melting ice to the diesel engine

records.title: From an uncertain orbit to variation between people
records.description: What changes when scatter belongs to the population?
terms: From an uncertain orbit to variation between people

Repeated measurements of one object and measurements of different people generate different kinds of variation. Explain which uncertainty a fitted line describes in each case and what it cannot establish about inheritance.
From errors in an orbit to inherited stature

records.title: Chemical order and an unexpected product
records.description: When should a familiar classification be challenged?
terms: Chemical order and an unexpected product
Use the periodic table to predict how an element should behave. Then ask what independent observation would justify revisiting an identification that appeared chemically reasonable.
How the periodic table hid the splitting of uranium

records.title: Food preservation and competing explanations
records.description: Can a process work reliably before its cause is known?
terms: Compare evidence that stored food lasts longer with evidence for a particular account of spoilage. A successful preservation trial answers the first question while leaving several possible explanations for the second.

records.title: From a compass deflection to a radio receiver
records.description: What does it take to turn an effect into a signal?
terms: From a compass deflection to a radio receiver
A deflection detects a relation between a current and a magnetic field. A receiver also has to select and distinguish a signal. Trace the extra demands imposed by detection, transmission and noise.
From a compass needle beside a wire to the wireless valve

records.title: From pea counts to the chromosome
records.description: Which observations support a model of inheritance?
terms: From pea counts to the chromosome
Start with a predicted ratio and a sample of finite size. Then ask what evidence could locate a heritable change physically rather than merely describe a pattern in descendants.
From counted peas to mutations made with X-rays

records.title: Infinity and the limits of calculation
records.description: How does the existence of a solution differ from a procedure to find it?
terms: Infinity and the limits of calculation
Separate a proof that a task has a finite answer from an algorithm that will always terminate with that answer. State where practical running time enters as a third question.
From the sizes of infinity to the limits of secrecy

records.title: From radiation to a particle track
records.description: What does an equation predict before a detector supplies a trace?
terms: From radiation to a particle track
Compare the role of a mathematical solution with the role of curvature in an observed track. Identify an instrumental ambiguity that could survive agreement with the prediction.
From a radiation formula to the anti-electron

records.title: Field comparisons and clinical trials
records.description: Which comparison could distinguish an intervention from a favourable starting point?
terms: Draw the groups before looking at outcomes. Mark when random allocation takes place, who can drop out and which population the comparison can support.
From field plots to a pandemic drug trial

records.title: Refrigeration and the Antarctic spring
records.description: How did a local industrial choice become a planetary measurement?
terms: Follow the chain from a useful manufactured substance to a proposed atmospheric mechanism and a seasonal map. Identify which link can be tested by comparing Antarctic observations across years.
From a safer refrigerator to the Antarctic spring

records.title: From dyes to medicines
records.description: When does a promising laboratory observation become evidence about patients?
terms: Distinguish finding an effect, obtaining a consistent substance, and comparing outcomes in people. A result at one of these stages does not supply the missing comparison at another.
From a red dye to a mould on Kyoto rice

records.title: From electronic calculation to climate prediction
records.description: What happens when a physical model runs on a finite grid?
terms: From electronic calculation to climate prediction
Compare a continuous process with its numerical approximation. Repeat a calculation with a shorter time step and distinguish numerical convergence from agreement with observations.

records.title: From gene regulation to a medical claim
records.description: Which evidence connects a molecular observation to an outcome?
terms: From gene regulation to a medical claim

Separate changes in expression, a proposed biological explanation and patient benefit. Ask how variation between cells affects the inference from their average and what separate evidence a therapeutic claim would require.
From RNA silencing to a programmable DNA cut

records.title: Making a decision in its own time
records.description: Choose a case. Write the decision you would make with the evidence available at the stated date, then identify the observation most likely to change it. Modern teaching supplies methods for checking your reasoning. In the Kindle edition, open Historical judgement. The headings below match the book’s contents.
terms: Can the instructions carry the calculation?
Which calculation does the problem require?
Which way did the particle travel?
How strong is the case for DNA in 1944?
An observation on a culture plate
What should follow a promising culture plate?
Could one shadow establish the size of Earth?
Plan a network conversion in November 1981
What does a second prism establish in 1672?
Would you accept an answer with a negative square root?
An old channel or a new one
In 100 BCE, would you reopen a channel or dig a new one?
Does the deepest ice still preserve time?
Would you fund the next seafloor test?
Which mortar would you specify for a wet repair?
In 1687, what would make Suriname’s rice usable?
What would Lind’s comparison justify in 1753?
When has an ocean cable succeeded?
Choose a field comparison before the harvest
Would reusable characters repay their preparation?
In 1866, what would you test after reading Mendel?
What would distinguish a carbon cage?
How much confidence should a comet prediction earn?
1086: Is a low-value mill worth repairing?
What can currents and needles establish in 1820?
A bound on an ether model
What did the ether experiment rule out?
What would birch tar prove in 2019?
How should a laboratory combine its programs?

records.title: A connected history of science and technology
records.description: Explore the history of science and technology from the earliest surviving tools to November 2026. Each period pairs historical questions with museum objects, university teaching or observational records.
